<!--BACKPORT [{"author":{"name":"Nikita Indik","email":"nikita.indik@elastic.co"},"sourceCommit":{"committedDate":"2026-09-21T13:55:59Z","message":"[Security Solution] Fix rule PATCH API silently ignoring type-specific fields when `type` is omitted (#288917)

## Summary

**Closes https://github.com/elastic/kibana/issues/287579**

This PR fixes an issue with the detection rules PATCH endpoint, where in
some cases the endpoint ignores type-specific fields if you don't pass
`type` in request parameters. Even though `type` is optional.

For example, if you tried to patch a `new_terms` rule and only passed
`id`/`rule_id` and `new_terms_fields` (no explicit `type: new_terms`) in
patch request, `new_terms_fields` would be ignored, rule won't be
updated and the endpoint would return 200.

### Cause

Without explicitly passed `type` Zod validation in route always
identified the patched rule as "EQL" and stripped all non-EQL properties
from it.

The route validated the body against the `RulePatchProps` union *before*
the existing rule was fetched. Since everything is optional in a patch
body, a typeless body matched the union's first branch (EQL), and
strip-mode parsing dropped every field that branch doesn't know about.

### Fix

Validate only non-type specific props in the route, let the
type-specific validation happen once the rule is fetched and its type is
known.

The route boundary now validates only the type-independent (shared)
props, via `SharedPatchRuleRequestBody` (`SharedPatchProps.loose()`),
and preserves type-specific fields as-is. Everything else was already in
place: `patchTypeSpecificParams` validates the body against the existing
rule type's patch schema, which is exactly where the rule type is known.

### Known gap (not fixed here)

A type-specific field sent for the *wrong* rule type is still ignored
rather than rejected: the per-type `*PatchFields` schemas are plain
`z.object`s, so `{ rule_id, threshold: {...} }` against a `query` rule
drops `threshold` and returns 200. That is unchanged by this PR — the
same request was a no-op before, with the field stripped at the route
boundary instead of in the per-type parse.

#### Other changes

- The threshold-cardinality and threat-mapping checks moved out of
`validatePatchRuleRequestBody` into `patchTypeSpecificParams` (which
happens later in the pipeline). Why: `validatePatchRuleRequestBody`
happens before the type is known, so if a user omits `type` in request,
these validations don't do anything. Once they are moved to
`patchTypeSpecificParams`, the `type` is knows, so these validations can
work properly. Related tests also moved.
- `patchRule` resolves the rule type for the ML authz check from the
existing rule rather than from `rulePatch.type` (which might not exist
or can be incorrect). PATCH cannot change a rule's type, so it makes
sense to read type from the existing rule.

### Behavior changes

Most of these are requests that used to be silent no-ops and now do
something, so this is a behavior change for external API consumers:

| Request | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Typeless patch of a type-specific field | 200, field ignored | 200,
change applied |
| Unknown/invalid `type` value | 400 (union error listing all types) |
400 (error for the existing rule's type) |
| Typeless threshold patch violating the cardinality rule | 200,
accepted | 400 |
| Typeless threat_match patch with a negate-only mapping | 200, accepted
| 400 |
| `threshold.field` sent as a string whose value contains the
cardinality field as a substring | 400 (spurious) | 200, accepted |
| `type: 'machine_learning'` sent for a non-ML rule without an ML
license | 403 (ML license error) | 400 (type mismatch) |

Kibana's own UI is unaffected: its `patchRule` helper has four call
sites, all of which patch `exceptions_list`, and the rule edit flow
deliberately uses PUT instead — see the note above `patchRule` in
`public/detection_engine/rule_management/api/api.ts`.

### Identify risks

- **Behavior change for external API consumers.** Requests that were
previously accepted as no-ops now either apply a change or fail with a
400.
- **Response shape change for two validation errors.** The cardinality
and negate-mapping 400s return `message` as a string instead of an
array, because those checks moved from the route's list-returning
validator into `patchTypeSpecificParams`. Clients that treat `message`
as an array for these specific errors would need updating. Every other
error body is unchanged.
- **A type-change attempt without an ML license now reports the type
mismatch.** The ML license gate is keyed on the rule being patched
rather than on the `type` in the request body, since PATCH cannot change
a rule's type. `type: 'machine_learning'` aimed at a non-ML rule
therefore returns 400 instead of 403. Patching a rule that actually is
ML still returns 403 without the license.
- **Error precedence change against missing rules.** An unknown `type`
value, or a malformed type-specific field, on a nonexistent `rule_id`
now yields 404 rather than 400, since the rule is read before
type-specific validation. Both were already error paths.
- **Unknown keys now reach the RBAC check.** The route no longer strips
keys it does not recognize, so they survive into the read-auth branch in
`patchRule` and force the full-privileges path. A read-only user
patching a read-auth field plus a stray key now gets a 403 where they
used to get a 200. Garbage in, error out — and it would become a 400 if
the known gap above is ever closed.

author: chaseflorell
body:
Authentication was a placeholder end to end. `AuthContext.tsx` wrote a `sessionStorage` marker; both the credential form and the "Continue with Google" button called the same no-op; `AdminGate.cs` accepted any non-empty `X-Hpac-Member-Session` header and said so in its own doc comment. `IMemberAuthenticator` had zero implementations, and `admin_users` was migrated but never read.

This records the decisions that replace all of that, and reconciles every specification page with them. **Docs only — no code.** Every new scenario lands `@ignore` and is un-ignored by the pull request that implements it.

## Decisions

| ADR | Decision |
|---|---|
| 0064 | JWT bearer authentication with three roles — `User`, `SafetyOfficer`, `Administrator`. The claim *name* is configuration; the claim *values* are invariant codes. The API reads the subject and the role and nothing else. **Supersedes ADR-0005.** The provider choice (Auth0 vs AWS Cognito) is explicitly deferred. |
| 0065 | No user records; identity is the token subject. `admin_users` is dropped and its two referencing columns become opaque strings. |
| 0066 | A development identity provider signed with a dev key, validated through the same middleware production uses. The SPA learns its mode from the API, never a build flag. |
| 0067 | A reporter must be a member, and is not recorded. |
| 0068 | The member token replaces Turnstile on submission. |

### The carved exception, stated plainly

ADR-0065 drops a table, which `AGENTS.md` invariant 8 and `manage-hpac-migrations` rule 3 forbid. The exception rests on one specific fact: **`admin_users` has never held application data in any deployed environment.** The only row any database ever received is the guarded synthetic `admin@localhost`, and production never sets the guard. The rule is unchanged for every table holding reports, answers, files, summaries, or audit entries, and the ADR says the exception does not generalize.

### The reversal worth reading carefully

ADR-0067 reverses "reporting is anonymous; no account required," which was asserted in seven places. Submission now requires a signed-in member **and records nothing about them** — no subject, no id, no hash, no join table. Authentication answers one question, *is this an HPAC member?*, and the answer is discarded. The form will say so to the reporter.

## Status and body edits

ADR-0005 superseded. ADR-0020, ADR-0040, and ADR-0048 partially superseded — ADR-0040 also gains the `status:` frontmatter it never had, which an automated status audit would have missed. Body edits on 0010, 0018, 0019, 0031, 0033, 0034, 0042, 0051, and 0063. ADR-0063 is notable: it explicitly anticipated this decision ("the owner's position is that the form will require authentication; that decision is not made by this ADR"), and now records that it has been.

## Scenarios

Of the moderation feature's 30 scenarios: **9 deleted** (third-party sign-in through the port, cookie issuance, credential proxying, allowlist disclosure, admin revocation, allowlist management, stale allowlist concurrency, admin soft-deletion), **4 rewritten**, 11 unaffected. New untagged scenarios cover token validation failures, the three-role authoring matrix, and that no claim beyond the subject and role is ever read. New `@ui` scenarios cover role-aware menus and the development login page.

Report submission gains a member-token precondition, loses Turnstile, and gains four scenarios asserting the submitter is not recorded.

**Four `@ui` scenarios continue to run unchanged. Two are parked** — the login-page and Admin-menu scenarios describe behavior that does not exist yet, so they carry `@ignore` until #192 builds the token-bearing session. `bddgen` was run to confirm the remaining active set has no undefined steps.

## Deliberately not in this PR

The homepage copy saying reports "can be filed anonymously" is **still true today** and stays until #193 ships the behavior and the qualifier together. Changing it now would make it false.

## Follow-on work

#190 drops `admin_users` · #191 adds JWT validation and role policies · #192 builds the web session · #193 lands authenticated, unattributed submission.

## Open questions

1. `officer`/`officer` as the SafetyOfficer development credential is my recommendation, not yet ruled.
2. Confirm a signed-in `User` sees logout and nothing else. "My reports" is impossible by construction.
3. Should a 403 write an audit row carrying the subject, or only a log line?
4. Public feed reading is assumed to stay anonymous; nothing here changes it.

No .feature scenario needed: this pull request is the .feature change.

Closes #189

body:
# Release 0.0.5


### Added
- The integration tests to test Packit.
- The build scripts now get the `PACKIT_BUILD_JOBS_COUNT` variable to use for parallel builds and tests.
- The uninstall now uninstalls packages in the correct order (so dependents before dependencies).
- The `--exclude` flag for the `pit util package` command, to exclude certain packages when using the `--all` flag.
- New and improved documentation.
- The notice fields in the metadata to show a message before or after an installation.
- The local metadata storage, which stores the metadata of installed packages. (BREAKING)
- Parsing for target additions, which doesn't allow for empty additions or additions with invalid characters.
- License identifiers are now checked for invalid characters and being empty.
- The `PACKIT_DISABLE_PROMPTS` environment variable, which triggers an error when Packit tries to prompt.
- The `LocalMetadataExistence` verifier check.
- The `config reset` command, to reset the Packit configuration file to its default.
- Caching of the metadata from all requests to metadata repositories.
- The verifier can now recover parts of syntactically wrong toml files, specifically the `Config.toml` and `Register.toml`.
- Support for multiple repositories conflict checking, using the `compatible_repositories` field in the `Config.toml` and `repository.toml`. (BREAKING)
- The checks for paths defined in the metadata that escape their parent directory.

### Changes
- The build tests are now turned off by default and can be turned on with `--execute-build-test` (`--skip-build-test` is removed).
- Package names are now always lowercase, the commands translate uppercase to lowercase. (BREAKING)
- The parsing for dependencies and targets bounds doesn't allow for `name@` anymore. (BREAKING)
- The `pit util meta-check` command now returns a different exit code, dependending on the most urgent issue type found.
- The `pit init` command now allows you to specify the revision of the Packit install.
- The package resolver now skips repository compatibility checks if the package is `packit`.
- Update all dependencies to their latest available versions.

### Fixed
- Fix patch apply directory meta check reporting wrong issues.
- Fix patches being able to change files outside of the build directory.
- Fix the `license_include` file being able to include a file outside of the build directory.
- Fix build environment to also add symlinked packages in `CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH` and `ACLOCAL_PATH`.
- Fix `pit switch-dependency` command not checking if dependency is still satisfied.
- Fix the tree cycle check, it now also checks cycles to the root.
- Fix the target priority calculations, now the priority for os or architectures with an addition and version are also correctly calculated.
- Fix double recursion display for the licenses.
- Fix the `include_license` field resolving symlinks, now they are not resolved anymore.
- Fix errors in command not resulting in non-zero exit code.
- Fix update functionality checking if dependency is still satisfied in a wrong way.
- Fix the re-install fix in the repairer uninstalling a package when it cannot be installed.

author: moltycel
body:
## What

`developers.html` said credentials are Merkle-batched and anchored on Base L2. It never said how the 32 bytes in the calldata are derived — so a holder could read the Merkle proof we stored beside their credential, but could not recompute the leaf that proof starts from. The leaf was our assertion, not their check. A bounty submission found this, and it was paid.

This specifies the encoding and ships it in three forms: prose, a worked example against a real transaction, and a runnable verifier.

- `docs/spec-fakten/anchor-commitment.md` — leaf preimage for both `MolTrust/VC/v1` and `MolTrust/IPR/v1`, timestamp serialization, tree construction and the padding rule, the calldata envelope, proof replay, and what the anchor does and does not establish.
- `scripts/verify_anchor.py` — the same encoding, executable. Imports nothing from this repository, needs no API key, reads a public RPC endpoint.
- `app/provenance/anchor.py` — anchors now write `evidence[0].credentialId`.
- `migrations/2026-09-21_evidence_credential_id.sql` — backfills that field on the 261 already-anchored credentials. Additive and idempotent; nothing that feeds a leaf is touched, so no root moves.

## Two defects the verification found

The acceptance test for this work was to write a verifier from the documentation alone, without consulting `anchor.py`, and run it against the chain. That exercise found two real problems, both of which would have made the documentation worse than useless:

**The document did not carry `cred_id`.** It is the first field of the leaf preimage and appeared nowhere in the credential — so the promise "you can recompute this yourself" was false as written. Fixed by `credentialId` in the evidence block, forward and backfilled.

**Two W3C data model versions, two timestamp fields, two UTC designators.** 187 of 261 credentials use `validFrom` (credentials/v2), 74 use `issuanceDate` (credentials/v1). One renders its offset as `+00:00` rather than `Z`. A verifier reading `validFrom` crashes on a third of the set; one that strips a trailing `Z` unconditionally computes the wrong leaf for the rest. The spec reads `proof.created`, which is present in both, and handles both designators.

A third came out of implementing the tree from my own prose: written as "pad odd levels while reducing", the algorithm returns the bare leaf for a one-credential batch instead of `SHA-256(leaf ‖ leaf)`. The leaf level is padded once, before the reduction loop. `0x40d872fa…` is that case, and the spec now says so explicitly.

## Verification

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Leaf recomputed from the document, path replayed, root compared to on-chain calldata | 261 of 261 credentials, across 15 transactions |
| Whole batch rebuilt from its documents, root compared to calldata | 15 of 15 batches |
| IPR namespace, same check | `0x142b8c1e…` recomputed and matched |

Worked example in the spec is `0xa5f77cb7…`, block 51 604 928 — three credentials, so the padding rule is visible in the output.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

## Fix: AI proxy model allowlist (#1985)

Adds a per-provider server-side model allowlist to prevent arbitrary model ID injection.

### Changes
- factory.ts: Added PROVIDER_ALLOWED_MODELS map with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google models. zaic/custom are open. Added isModelAllowed validator.
- route.ts: Validates model ID against provider allowlist. Rejects unknown model IDs with HTTP 400 + INVALID_MODEL.

### Security
Fixes high-severity issue where arbitrary model IDs could be passed without server-side validation.

## Summary by Sourcery

Enforce per-provider AI model allowlists to prevent arbitrary model ID injection through the AI proxy.

Bug Fixes:
- Reject unsupported model IDs with a clear HTTP 400 INVALID_MODEL response before processing AI proxy requests.

Enhancements:
- Add server-side, per-provider model validation while keeping zaic and custom providers open to backend-defined models.

Cette PR ajoute une commande d’opérateur sur le binaire backend, et une vraie page `/recover`. ## Après déploiement Lister les comptes (pour retrouver l’identifiant admin) : ```bash docker exec -it luna-backend ./luna-backend users # bare metal, depuis backend/src avec le même environnement que le service : ./luna-backend users ``` Définir un nouveau mot de passe (saisie masquée, ou `LUNA_NEW_PASSWORD` sans TTY) : ```bash docker exec -it luna-backend ./luna-backend reset-password TON_IDENTIFIANT ``` Si plus aucun compte n’est administrateur : ```bash docker exec -it luna-backend ./luna-backend promote-admin TON_IDENTIFIANT ``` `reset-password` réactive le compte et invalide toutes ses sessions. Ne jamais passer le mot de passe en argument (historique shell). Les commandes doivent utiliser le même `DATA_PATH` et la même base que le backend, sinon le pepper de hash ne correspond pas. ## Contenu - `luna-backend users` / `reset-password` / `promote-admin` - Page `/recover` avec les instructions opérateur - Documentation dans `documentation/deployment.md`

author: seriouslysean
body:
Paired with an agent on this.

> **Releases.** `package.json` is the source of truth and the bump always arrives inside a PR, because `main` is protected (required `ci` check) and the repo has no PAT, so nothing can push a bump commit after a merge.
> - `update-data.yml` bumps the version in the data PR it already opens: MINOR for a new Minecraft feature version (26.3 → 26.4), PATCH for anything else.
> - New `release.yml` runs after CI passes on `main` (the same `workflow_run` trigger as the deploy, since `GITHUB_TOKEN` merges never fire `push`). When `package.json` is ahead of the latest `v*` tag it creates the annotated tag and a release with generated notes, titled `vX.Y.Z (Minecraft <data version>)`. Anything else is a no-op.
> - AGENTS.md gains a "Releases" section defining the SemVer buckets; dependency/CI/docs changes don't release.
>
> **Parse.** `generate()` collects per-recipe failures and throws them together, so one failed update run lists everything that changed shape.
>
> Bumps to 1.0.1 so this merge exercises the release path end to end.
>
> Test: after merge, CI on main → `Release` workflow → `v1.0.1` tag + release. `npm test` covers the aggregate throw.
>
> Closes #10

author: jdx
body:
<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/pitchfork/trails/26
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Scheduled daemons can have no process running between executions, making process status alone insufficient to check their timing. `pitchfork status <daemon>` now shows the cron expression, most recent recorded scheduled start, and next scheduled time, with relative times for quick inspection.

For a daily backup:

```toml
[daemons.backup]
run = "./scripts/backup.sh"
cron = { schedule = "0 0 2 * * *", retrigger = "finish" }
```

Run `pitchfork status backup` to inspect its timing. `Last run: never` means no scheduled start has been recorded; manual starts, skipped executions, and attempts that fail to spawn a process do not update it. Historical runs from before this feature are not reconstructed.

`Next run` shows when the supervisor will next evaluate the schedule, subject to the retrigger policy. A due time that has passed is labeled `overdue`, including when the supervisor was stopped across a scheduled time. The daemon's `Status` remains separate: it may reflect a later manual execution and does not necessarily describe the run named by `Last run`.

Timing is also available in the TUI detail pane and as `cron_schedule`, `cron_last_run`, and `cron_next_run` in CLI JSON and HTTP API daemon entries. Timestamps use RFC 3339 in JSON; unavailable values are omitted from CLI JSON and returned as `null` by the HTTP API.

The scheduling guide now explains how to interpret these fields, overdue times, and JSON output.

Validation: `mise run ci-dev` passed, including lint, generated references, the documentation build, 1,526 Rust tests, and 405 shell integration tests.

Closes #901

*AI-assisted — Tool: Codex; model: OpenAI/GPT-6; version: unavailable.*

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Mostly read-path and observability; adds optional state persistence on cron spawns with sync writes, without changing core retrigger or watcher trigger rules beyond recording runs.
> 
> **Overview**
> Adds **cron schedule visibility** when a scheduled daemon is stopped between runs: `pitchfork status`, the TUI detail pane, CLI `--json`, and the HTTP API now expose the expression plus **last scheduled start** and **next due time**, with human-readable relative times (including **overdue** for missed windows).
> 
> **Last run** is a new persisted field (`last_cron_run`), written synchronously when the cron watcher actually **spawns** a process (`cron_started`), not on manual starts, skipped ticks, or pre-spawn failures. It is separate from `last_cron_triggered`. **Next run** is computed via `Daemon::next_cron_run`, aligned with the watcher’s anchoring (`immediate` lookback, last tick, missed windows). Config-only placeholders can show the schedule before the supervisor registers the daemon.
> 
> Shared formatting lives in `ui/cron::format_at`. The scheduling guide documents how to read these fields and JSON. Integration tests cover status/JSON behavior.
> 
> <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit ef2496e7d1afcbd7c9b546519a4f4fbb797b96d9. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup>

author: felddy
body:
## 🗣 Description

Bundles the official [Foundry VTT CLI](https://github.com/foundryvtt/foundryvtt-cli) in the image as the `fvtt` command, pre-configured for the container's installation and data paths.

Closes #654

## 💭 Motivation and context

The upstream blockers noted in #654 are resolved: the CLI gained a local-config mechanism (foundryvtt/foundryvtt-cli#50), and it honors `XDG_DATA_HOME` on Linux. Meanwhile, since npm was removed from the final image, users can no longer install the CLI themselves — bundling is now the only reasonable way to support the module-development workflows the issue describes.

Design notes:

- **Isolated build stage** — the CLI's `classic-level` dependency ships prebuilt native bindings for amd64/arm64 only; on ppc64le and s390x it compiles via node-gyp. The toolchain (g++, make, python3) lives only in the `fvtt-cli-stage`; the final image receives just the installed package (~9 MB).
- **Wrapper script** (`src/fvtt.sh` → `/usr/local/bin/fvtt`) — the CLI creates its config file on every invocation at `$XDG_DATA_HOME/.fvttrc.yml` (falling back to `~/.local/share`), which is not writable when the container runs as an arbitrary UID (the concern raised in [#654 (comment)](https://github.com/felddy/foundryvtt-docker/issues/654#issuecomment-1775049688)). The wrapper defaults `XDG_DATA_HOME` to `/data/.local/share` — writable for any UID and persistent — and seeds `installPath`/`dataPath` on first use, so `docker exec <container> fvtt ...` works with zero setup. The override is scoped to the CLI process; the Foundry server never sees it.
- **Renovate** — a new custom regex manager tracks the pinned `FOUNDRYVTT_CLI_VERSION` Dockerfile ARG against the npm registry.

## 🧪 Testing

- New container tests (`tests/test_fvtt_cli.py`): reported version matches the pinned version, seeded config paths are correct, `fvtt configure` reports a complete configuration, and the CLI works under a non-default UID (`12345:12345`).
- Verified locally: image builds and all 4 new tests pass (plus the existing non-credentialed suite).
- Documentation rendered via `render-docs-update`.

## ✅ Checklist

- [x] This PR has an informative and human-readable title.
- [x] Changes are limited to a single goal — no scope creep.
- [x] All relevant type-of-change labels have been added.
- [x] Documentation has been updated as needed.
- [x] Tests have been added or updated as needed.

## Summary
- `ADLogger.log()` resolves AutoDeploy-specific severities (`verbose`, `internal_error`) via `_SEVERITY_TO_LEVEL`, but `__init__()` and `set_level()` instead used `getattr(logging, level_str, logging.INFO)`. Since the standard `logging` module has no `VERBOSE`/`INTERNAL_ERROR` attributes, both names silently fell back to `INFO` in those two paths.
- This meant `AUTO_DEPLOY_LOG_LEVEL=verbose`/`internal_error` and `ADLogger().set_level("verbose"/"internal_error")` could never select `DEBUG`/`CRITICAL`, even though `log()` handled them correctly.
- Routes `__init__()` and `set_level()` through the same `_SEVERITY_TO_LEVEL` map `log()` already uses, so all three paths resolve severities consistently.

Fixes #19491

author: thomasbardhi01
body:
Diagnosis of the second Seaport failure, from the prod decisions row (pulled on the machine): `garage_search_error` → `{error: "parse_failed", detail: "HTTP 400"}` with tool input `starts_at: "2024-01-09T18:00:00"` — **the model hallucinated the date**. Nothing told it what "tonight" is, so it reached for a training-era default; SpotHero 400s past windows (`"requested start time is too far in the past"`, verified live). **Not** an IP block: the same query with a correct date returns 200 from Fly and from the Mac alike — the Mac/prod difference was the date, not the egress. The 403/429 contingencies (README note, device-side-search issue) therefore don't apply.

Fix:
- Every user turn carries `[current time: Mon 2026-01-05 14:00 ET]` (injectable clock), and the system prompt pins that all relative dates compute from it.
- `search_garages` and `quote_street` reject a start >1 h in the past with a corrective error **containing the current time**, so the model retries correctly in the same turn; the bounce is audited (`past_window`) and never reaches the provider.
- Tests (+3, 294 total): the verbatim prod transcript — hallucinated 2024 window → bounce → corrected retry → plan proposed, provider untouched by the bad request; the time line in every stored turn; the guard boundary.

author: phicks-debug
body:
## Summary

History loads in pages of 512 rows. Once tool results are stored (next PR), a page of large rows can cross Convex's per-query read limit and the conversation stops loading.

- `listConversationEvents` walks the index and closes a page at 512 rows or about 4 MiB of events, whichever comes first.
- Sizes come from convex's `getConvexSize`, the same count the read limit uses.
- The first row of a page always lands, so one row larger than the budget still moves the cursor.

## Description

A normal conversation is one round trip again: 500 text rows fit one page. Only a conversation heavy with tool output splits, and it splits where the read limit would have been hit. Args and the `{ page, isDone, continueCursor }` shape are unchanged, so core needs no change and deploy order does not matter.

An earlier revision of this PR dropped the page to 64 rows. That made 500 rows 8 sequential trips on every turn, and 65 rows of 1 MiB still crossed the limit.

## Verification

Focused: `packages/convex/tests/runtime.test.ts`. 513 small rows come back as a page of 512 and a page of 1. Seven 900 KiB rows split 5 and 2 by bytes, and the cursor carries on with no row skipped or repeated.

`bun run --filter @broods/convex check`, `bun run --filter @broods/core check`, root `bun run lint` (exit 0), `bun run format:check`: all clean. Convex suite 439 pass.

Stack 17 of 26. Base: `fix/ephemeral-subagent-session`. Builds on #585. Two commits. Merge in order; after a merge, retarget the next PR to `dev`.

body: ## Problem Opening the site showed **"خطأ اتصال — خطأ في الاتصال بسيرفر الفنادق"**. That toast (`js/hotels.js`) only fires when the request to the backend fails at the network level (connection refused / non-JSON error page) — i.e. the backend wasn't responding. Root cause: `server.listen(...)` was **inside** `mongoose.connect(MONGO_URI).then(...)`. So if MongoDB didn't connect on Render (paused free Atlas cluster, Atlas IP allowlist not including Render's egress IP, or rotated credentials), the HTTP server **never started** and the entire site went down — including static pages and search. ## Fix (`server.js`) - **Always `server.listen()` immediately**, independent of the DB. - **Connect to MongoDB in the background with automatic retry** (exponential-ish backoff, capped at 30s) + `disconnected`/`reconnected` logging. Now a DB hiccup degrades gracefully instead of taking the whole site down. RateHawk search still works via SERP (static content just falls back to the placeholder name until the DB reconnects), Dubai Link still works, and the site/homepage stay responsive. ## Verification (MongoDB made unreachable to simulate the Render outage) ``` boot: "🚀 السيرفر ... يعمل" then "❌ MongoDB connection failed (attempt 1) ... Retrying in 2s" LISTENING ✅ (previously: NOT listening -> site down) GET / -> 200 GET /api/v1/health-check -> 200 POST /api/v1/hotels/search -> 200 (RateHawk SERP results; names fall back to "فندق شريك لرمال وفلّها" until DB is back) ``` With a healthy DB it connects normally: "✅ MongoDB Database Connected Successfully!". ## If the site is still down after deploying this The remaining likely causes are outside the code — please check on Render/Atlas: 1. **MongoDB Atlas Network Access**: allowlist `0.0.0.0/0` (or Render's static egress IP). A paused free Atlas cluster must be resumed. 2. **Render env vars**: `MONGO_URI` (Atlas SRV), `RATEHAWK_BASE_URL` (+ prod region via `RATEHAWK_DEFAULT_REGION_ID`/`RATEHAWK_DESTINATION_REGION_MAP`), `RATEHAWK_KEY_ID`/`RATEHAWK_API_KEY`, `FRONTEND_URL`. 3. **Render deploy status/logs**: confirm the latest deploy succeeded and the service is awake (free tier spins down when idle; first request cold-starts).

author: jfcastro92
body:
Fixes #3910.

## The bug

Opening a file through a URL — `/app/<name>?file=<path or uid>` — puts a consent prompt in front of the user, because the link chose both the app and the file. That prompt was shown **unconditionally**: Allow wrote an `fs:<uid>:write` grant against the app, and the next launch of the same link never read it. Same link, same file, same app, prompt every time.

The sibling flows already settled themselves from existing grants — the popup permission flow checks first (`initgui.js`), and `puter.ui.requestPermission` pre-checks in the SDK (`UI.js`). The URL-launch gate was the one site that didn't.

## The change

- **`/auth/check-permissions` takes an optional `app_uid`** — the account asking what one of *its apps* holds, rather than what it holds itself. The app-under-user actor is built the same way the grant handlers resolve theirs (uid-or-name), so a check answers for exactly the app a grant would name.
- **`appHoldsPermissions(permissions, appUid)`** in `holdsPermissions.js`, next to the existing token-based helper, sharing one round trip. A launch has no app token yet, so it asks as the user and names the app.
- **`confirmUrlFileAccess`** skips the dialog when the grant is already held, and still returns the stat'd file so the app opens with it.

Denials are unchanged: "Don't Allow" writes nothing, so the next launch asks again.

## Security callout

This adds a permission read and widens nothing:

- `app_uid` is **sessions only** — an app actor or a scoped access token gets a 403. Without that gate, any app could enumerate which grants its neighbours hold under the same user.
- Unknown app → 404; `app_uid` present but not a non-empty string (`""`, `null`, a non-string) → 400. Both before any check runs. The empty case is deliberately *not* treated as "no app": falling through to the user would answer `true` for every `fs:` scope on a file they own, settling a prompt nobody answered.
- The GUI helper **refuses to ask without an app uid**. That guard is the load-bearing one: asked as the user alone, the user's own file answers `true`, which would skip the prompt entirely. The test run below shows exactly that asymmetry (`true` as the user, `false` as the app).
- Every failure mode is fail-closed — no token, empty list, non-2xx, timeout, network error all report "not held" and the prompt runs.
- The consent gate itself is untouched: a file the app has no grant on still prompts, and a directory is still refused outright.

## Test results

### Browser, end to end (local server, Playwright, fresh app + file per run)

Same `/app/<name>?file=…` link visited three times.

Before (fix reverted, bundle rebuilt):

```
file /admin/Desktop/put1865-1790016740002.txt -> e3a412d7-6b43-4c44-b063-248b57c36631
app put1865-1790016740099 -> app-6f7b16f5-3f16-459a-a585-081368be1141
first-visit: permission dialog SHOWN
first-visit: allowed
second-visit: permission dialog SHOWN
third-visit: permission dialog SHOWN

FAIL — expected SHOWN, not shown, not shown
```

After:

```
file /admin/Desktop/put1865-1790016853600.txt -> 74b84fd9-f5a3-4f25-8732-656e5cd0857b
app put1865-1790016853687 -> app-6e032245-4455-415a-9429-914348249493
first-visit: permission dialog SHOWN
first-visit: allowed
first-visit: app opened with puter.item.name=put1865-1790016853600.txt
second-visit: permission dialog not shown
second-visit: app opened with puter.item.name=put1865-1790016853600.txt
third-visit: permission dialog not shown
third-visit: app opened with puter.item.name=put1865-1790016853600.txt

PASS — asked once, remembered after that
```

The `puter.item.name` line is the check that skipping the prompt doesn't quietly drop the file — the app still opens with it.

<!-- SCREENSHOTS -->

### The endpoint over HTTP (same server, real grant)

```
file check-perm-1790016481106.txt -> a1f02993-bd4f-4434-9fd1-f63279fed015
app -> app-3b7cdd0e-2489-4bd6-96b8-29ca7bc88b9d
as the user (owns the file): {"permissions":{"fs:a1f02993-...:write":true}}
as the app, before grant:    {"permissions":{"fs:a1f02993-...:write":false}}
as the app, after grant:     {"permissions":{"fs:a1f02993-...:write":true}}
unknown app:                 404 {"error":"App app-00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000000 does not exist",...}

PASS
```

### Suites

```
$ npx vitest run --config src/backend/vitest.config.ts src/backend/controllers/auth/AuthController.test.ts
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  352 passed (352)

$ npx vitest run --config src/backend/vitest.config.ts src/backend/services/permission src/backend/drivers/driverPolicies.test.ts
 Test Files  5 passed (5)
      Tests  224 passed (224)

$ npx vitest run --config src/gui/vitest.config.js
 Test Files  63 passed (63)
      Tests  802 passed (802)

$ npm run typecheck
Type check passed — no new errors (30 known, baselined).
```

New coverage, each failing before the fix:

- `AuthController.test.ts` — `app_uid` answers `false` for the app while `true` for the asking user, then `true` once granted; an app actor asking gets 403; unknown app 404; non-string `app_uid` 400; `""`/`null` 400 while an omitted key still answers about the user.
- `confirmUrlFileAccess.test.js` — hands the file over without constructing the dialog when the grant is held; prompts when the check throws.
- `holdsPermissions.test.js` — asks as the user with `app_uid` in the body; reports not held and sends nothing when no app is named.

## Review round

`/code-review` raised four findings; three are fixed in `ab7a5f3`, the fourth is scoped out deliberately.

- **Fixed — a present-but-empty `app_uid` answered about the user.** `app_uid ? … : req.actor` read `""`/`null` as "no app", and on a file the user owns the `is-owner` implicator makes every `fs:` scope `true` — so a client meaning "does app X hold this?" got `true` and skipped consent. Latent (the GUI guards twice, and the helper refuses to ask without a uid), but fail-open on an endpoint where everything else fails closed. Now a 400, with a regression test.
- **Fixed — the check sat outside any catch.** `confirmUrlFileAccess` did not wrap it and `launchApp` calls it outside its own `try`, so a *rejecting* check would have failed the whole app launch rather than falling through to the prompt. Only `queryHeld`'s internal catch stood behind it. Now caught locally, with the test asserting a throwing check still prompts (the previous test duplicated the not-held default and verified nothing).
- **Fixed — seam named for the wrong function.** The injectable defaulted to `appHoldsPermissions` but was called `holdsPermissions`; wiring the token-based sibling in would have sent an app uid as `Authorization: Bearer …`, 401'd, and degraded to always-prompting with nothing surfaced. Renamed to `appHoldsPermissions`.
- **Not fixed, follow-up — an ancestor grant still prompts per file.** Confirmed accurate: the ancestor walk lives in `ACLService.check` (`src/backend/services/acl/ACLService.ts:218`), not in `PermissionService.checkMany`, whose only ancestor-walking implicator is plain-user-only. So an app holding `fs:<folder uid>:write` is still prompted for each file inside it, and each Allow writes another per-file row. It is fail-safe (an extra prompt, never extra access) and it is a different shape from the reported bug — the ticket and the repro are both "same file, same link, asked again". Closing it properly means answering this check through ACL rather than the permission table, which changes what `puter.perms.holds` reports for app actors — a public SDK behavior change that deserves its own PR. Happy to file it as a follow-up ticket.

## Notes for the reviewer

- The check sits on the launch path with the helper's existing 5s timeout, so a stalled `/auth/check-permissions` delays the prompt by up to 5s before falling through to it. Same budget the popup flow already accepts.
- No SDK or docs surface changes: `app_uid` is a new optional field on an internal endpoint, `puter.perms`' own `checkPermissions` is untouched, and

author: ajiangny
body:
## Summary

Admins can now manage schedule **event types** (a name plus a color) from the Schedule tab, and 30-minute events show their name on the grid.

- **Event types.** New `schedule_event_types` table. Events point at a type through `schedule_events.type_id`, so recoloring a type recolors every event that uses it. A type that events still use cannot be deleted (FK `ON DELETE RESTRICT`, surfaced as a 409).
- **Colors.** The palette grows from 4 to 7: `pink` (default for the new **Workshop** type), `lime` (default for the new **Fun** type), and `tangerine` as a spare. Colors are picked from this fixed palette, not a free color picker, so every choice stays legible on the dark grid.
- **Admin UI.** New collapsible "Event Types" panel in the Schedule tab: add, rename, recolor, delete. Changes are staged and go through the same diff modal as events. The event modal's Color field is now a Type picker.
- **30-minute slots.** Events of 30 minutes or less render the event name only. Previously the clamped title shrank to zero height in the one-row block and only the time was visible. The hover tooltip still shows the time.
- **Admin refresh fix.** `apiFetch` now uses `cache: "no-store"`. The public GET routes send `stale-while-revalidate` for the CDN, which also let the browser answer the dashboard's post-save refetch from its HTTP cache, so saved changes only appeared after a manual refresh. Public pages are unaffected (they use `useApiData`).

## API

- `GET /api/schedule/types` (public), `POST /api/schedule/types`, `PUT /api/schedule/types/:id`, `DELETE /api/schedule/types/:id` (admin).
- `GET /api/schedule` still returns a flat `color` per event, now taken from the event's type, so the public site and the static fallback data are unchanged.
- `POST /api/schedule` requires `type_id`. `PUT /api/schedule/:id` now writes only known event fields instead of the raw request body.
- 422 for a color outside the palette or an unknown type, 409 when deleting a type in use.

## Database

Migration `20260921000000_schedule_event_types.sql`:

- Creates the table with RLS (public read, service-role full access) and a CHECK constraint on the palette.
- Adds `schedule_events.type_id` plus an index.
- Seeds the six default types and backfills `type_id` from each event's existing color. The seed only runs where events already exist (production, or a local `migration up`). On a `db reset` the events table is still empty at that point, so nothing is seeded and the types come from `seed.sql`; seeding unconditionally would duplicate them once the dump includes this table.
- `schedule_events.color` is kept as the fallback for rows without a type. It can be dropped in a follow-up.

**After `db push`, re-dump `seed.sql`** so local resets include the new table.

The palette is mirrored in `frontend/src/lib/scheduleColors.ts`, `backend/src/lib/scheduleColors.ts`, and the CHECK constraint; change all three together (documented in `docs/MASTER.md`).

## Verification

- `npm run lint` and `npm run build` pass in `frontend/`; `npm run build` passes and `npm run dev` boots in `backend/`.
- Applied locally with `migration up --local`: 6 types seeded, all 15 existing events backfilled. Replaying the migration SQL a second time is a no-op. `db lint --local` reports no errors.
- curl against the local API: types list returns, events carry their type's color, recoloring a type in the DB changes the color `GET /api/schedule` returns, unauthenticated writes get 401, and Postgres rejects deleting a type in use.
- Admin flow clicked through locally (add, recolor, assign, save, collapse).
- Not run: `db reset`, because the current local `seed.sql` predates the new table (see the note above).

author: jesuscabrera84
body:
El despliegue de `v1.32.1` falló en **400 ms**, y no por el bloqueo que buscábamos:

```
psycopg2.errors.ForeignKeyViolation
insert or update on table "organization_users" violates
constraint "organization_users_organization_id_fkey"
DETAIL: Key (organization_id)=(208ade42-…) is not present in table "organizations".
```

Producción quedó intacta: `/health` sigue en `028_identidad_esquema`, sirviendo `v1.31.0`.

## La premisa que resultó falsa

Se midió «siete usuarios con `is_master` y sin membresía OWNER» y se concluyó que eran **masters heredados**, de antes de que existiera `organization_users`. Al medir los huérfanos salieron **exactamente los mismos siete** — mismos ids, mismas organizaciones.

Y la causa es circular:

> **No tienen membresía porque su organización no existe.** `organization_users.organization_id` tiene FK a `organizations`, así que esa fila **nunca pudo crearse**. No son masters heredados: son **filas huérfanas**.

## Tres consecuencias

1. **El relleno inserta cero filas hoy**, y nunca iba a insertar otra cosa. Se conserva con el `EXISTS` porque es el invariante correcto y hará lo suyo si algún día aparece un master con organización real y sin membresía.
2. **El *fallback* de `is_master` se puede borrar sin relleno ninguno**, y por una razón más limpia: lo único que sostiene son huérfanos, a los que devuelve «OWNER de una organización que no existe». Al quitarlo pasan a `None` — que no es menos acceso, es el mismo dicho con verdad.
3. **`users.organization_id` no tiene clave foránea en producción.** El DDL sólo declara un índice; el modelo sí la declara. Es deriva que el comparador no ve porque mira columnas y no restricciones — **sobre la columna que 62 endpoints usan para decidir quién ve qué**. Añadir la FK exige resolver antes los siete huérfanos, y es trabajo aparte.

## Corrige además una afirmación falsa

El commit de la `029`, su entrada de CHANGELOG y el **PR #84** decían que una de las siete era la cuenta de Jesús y que *«quitar el fallback sin rellenar le habría costado el OWNER de su organización»*. **Es falso**: su organización no existe, así que el *fallback* sólo le daba OWNER de algo que no está.

## El test

`test_master_con_organizacion_inexistente_no_tumba_la_migracion`, **verificado quitando el `EXISTS`**: reproduce el `ForeignKeyViolation` exacto de producción. Es lo que convierte aquel fallo en algo que se ve en CI y no en un despliegue.

Batería completa **844 passed**, cobertura **74.81 %**.

## Lo que este PR NO hace

Los siete huérfanos siguen ahí. **Resolverlos es una operación de datos deliberada, no una migración** — borrar esas filas no es limpieza: veinte claves foráneas referencian `users`, varias con `ON DELETE CASCADE` hacia `mobility.devices`, `team.members`, `user_units` y `user_devices`, y otras sin `ON DELETE` que bloquearían el borrado desde `account_events`. La salida razonable es **desactivarlos** con la columna que esta misma migración añade.

author: hectorespert
body:
Applies `openspec/changes/size-the-log-ring-and-batch-its-flushes/`. **17 of 25 tasks.** Everything that does not need 35 hours of uptime or a power cut is done and verified on the board; what is left is named at the bottom, not buried.

## The measurement the change rested on, taken before changing anything

```
FAT32: cluster=32768 B (64 blocks) clusters=242304 fatBlocks=1894 fats=2
card=15523840 blocks (7580 MiB)
deleting 1048576 KiB: 32768 clusters, 256 FAT sectors, ~768 ops contiguous, <=98304 fragmented
deleting 1024 KiB:        32 clusters,   1 FAT sector,    ~3 ops contiguous, <=96 fragmented
```

Deleting a gigabyte is tens of seconds at the fragmented ceiling, against a `WDT_TIMEOUT_MS` of **1398**. So the latent watchdog reset was real rather than theoretical, and it belonged to the **1 GiB default** — unarmed only because filling a gigabyte at 34 B/s takes about a year. At 1 MiB the ceiling is ~48 ms: **safe at the ceiling, not merely at the contiguous floor**, which is stronger than the task asked for.

## What changed

- **Ring defaults: 4 × 1 MiB.** Footprint 4 GiB → 4 MiB, rotation every ~8.6 h, a file down the link in under four minutes.
- **`write()` syncs once per 4 KiB**, not once per record. That needed a structural change rather than a moved `flush()`: `write()` went through `writeRaw()`, and `writeRaw()` must keep syncing every call because it carries the `FMT` preamble — a preamble that does not reach the card costs the whole file rather than its tail. Appending is now a private `appendBytes()` both paths share; they differ only in when they sync.
- **No file under `src/` moved.** `src/sdwrite.cpp` constructs `SdData sdData;` with no arguments, so the new footprint arrives through the header.

## Three things came out differently from how the tasks described them

All three are recorded in `tasks.md` rather than quietly reconciled.

**The test's size constant had to be raised, not just renamed.** At 1024 bytes a rotation always arrived before the 4 KiB interval and `close()` synced, so **the suite could not exercise batching at all**. It is `TEST_FILE_SIZE_BYTES = 8192` now, with the rotation loops deriving their count from it. The rename closes the `TEST_FILE_SIZE_MB` item in *Minor leftovers cleanup*.

**Task 3.3 was untestable as written.** It asked for a case asserting the byte counter is reset at a rotation. It is reset — but carrying it across would only make the new file's first interval *shorter*, a smaller bound rather than a violated one, and nothing observable. The case asserts instead that a rotation does not lose what was accumulated but unsynced, which is what could genuinely break. It passes against the old flush too, so it is a regression guard and says so in its own comment.

**Headroom moved by 4 bytes**, 3184 → 3180. That is the `size_t` counter and nothing else. The task expected zero; four is the honest answer.

## Verification

| | |
|---|---|
| `pio test -e libs` | **20/20 in 23 s** — down from 43 s, which is measured evidence the card work fell |
| the interval case | **watched failing first** against the restored per-record flush, on its predicted message |
| `pio test` (HIL) | 25 passed, 8 skipped, 0 failed |
| `pio check` | 2 LOW, unchanged |
| `pio run` | headroom 3180 B |

## The HIL suite failed first, and the cause was not this change

Six flashes in a few minutes — chasing the `TEST_MESSAGE` output — none surviving the five-minute stability window, took the consecutive fault counter to **3 of 3** and latched the reduced configuration (`custom_mode` `0x05030603`, `state=5`, `base_mode=0x80` without `AUTO_ENABLED`). `TaskMavlink` then withholds `BATTERY_STATUS`, so `check_telemetry.py`'s `test_battery_status_every_2s` reported 0.00 Hz and **failed**, while `check_recovery.py`'s `test_heartbeat_reports_operational` **self-skipped correctly**.

That is the backlog entry *[`check_telemetry.py`'s `test_battery_status_every_2s` assumes the normal configuration]* firing for the first time: one case self-skips on that condition and its neighbour does not. `MAV_CMD_PREFLIGHT_REBOOT_SHUTDOWN` cleared both counters and restored the normal configuration at once, after which the suite passed.

Two things that cost time and are now in `CLAUDE.md`:

- **`pio test` hides `TEST_MESSAGE`.** It prints only pass/fail, so the report-only cases show nothing — including the two that predate this work, which have never displayed their figures through the documented command. `pio test -e libs -v` is required.
- **Check `custom_mode` *before* a series of reflashes**, because a latched reduced configuration makes the HIL suite fail in a way that reads as a regression in whatever you were working on.

## Left open, and why

- **1.2** — measuring a rotation at the old 1 GiB size. Writing a gigabyte at this library's throughput takes hours. An alternative exists (time `SD.remove()` at 1/4/16 MiB and extrapolate through the arithmetic already validated) and is not built.
- **5.1–5.6** — 35 hours of uninterrupted uptime so the ring comes all the way round, two power cuts on boards of different uptimes, and a card read. **Without 5.4 and 5.5 the requirement this change MODIFIES has no evidence at all**, and `tasks.md` says that in those words so it reaches the archive that way.
- **5.6** — the high-water marks have no baseline worth comparing against yet; see *Finish what make-sddata-begin-idempotent left open*, which records that the current figures are single samples.
- **6.3 / 6.4** — archive-time steps.

author: carlosverissimo3001
body:
Part of CAR-376. Frontend only, so it can ship without an API deploy.

## What broke

Since v2.3.0 (#228), a round starts with **no album art to unblur** and **no hints on its first round**. The cover box holds its grey placeholder alone.

`game/start` answers with `mapInitialGameState`: the session id, the ladder and the preview, and nothing else. The `game/:id` fetch that followed every start is what filled in the cover and the hints, and #228 removed it on the belief that the start already returned the whole state.

## What changes

- **After a start, the full state is fetched once again.** The trimmed state from the start still shows first, so the waiting frame appears instantly and fills in when the full one lands.
- **"Picking a song from undefined…"** is now "Picking a song…" when a playlist was opened by its link and its name has not loaded yet.

The proper fix is the other half of CAR-376: `game/start` returns the full state, as `game/:id` does, and this refetch goes again once no deployed client needs it.

author: darshanjainsde
body:
The database half of a full multi-tenant audit. Verified on staging first
(#97), which is where its two most interesting findings came from.

Report: https://claude.ai/artifact/UDy26zg1LqieEQfDnVpasN

## The boundary was never the problem

Row-level security is on all 134 tables and it holds. Six probes as the real
application role: read with no tenant set → 0 rows; list schools as school A →
only its own; fetch school B *by its exact id* → 0; insert a row stamped with
B's id → rejected; update B from A → 0 rows; and the tenant setting does not
survive `COMMIT`, so a transaction-pooled connection cannot carry it to the
next school. `/ready` answers `isolation: "enforced"` on both environments.

## What was broken was the cost of that design

Every policy compared `"schoolId"::text` to `current_setting(...)`. Casting the
**column** means a btree on a uuid column can never answer it, so `schoolId` sat
in the row Filter and never in the Index Cond — Postgres scanned the whole index,
or the whole table, and filtered afterwards. 129 of the 130 tenant tables already
carried an index leading with `schoolId`. They have been present and unreachable
since the first migration.

Measured on a 30-school, 7.2M-row copy of `Attendance`:

| the question a screen asks | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| one class's attendance for one month | 46 ms warm / 862 ms cold | 2 ms |
| `count(*)` for one school | 1,399 ms — Parallel Seq Scan, 6,960,000 rows discarded | 31 ms |
| newest 50 rows for one school | 1,271 ms | 37 ms |

The middle row is the one to read twice: the cost of *your* question was set by
everyone else's data. That is the noisy-neighbour law in a single query plan,
and it gets worse with every school onboarded.

`app_current_tenant()` is plain SQL so the planner inlines it — a plpgsql
function would not inline and the predicate would stop being an index condition.
`nullif(..., '')` is load-bearing, not decoration: a committed
`set_config(..., TRUE)` resets the GUC to the **empty string, not NULL**, so
without it the next statement on that pooled connection would raise on `''::uuid`.

**Nothing about who can see what changes.** Same column, same setting, same
fail-closed behaviour when it is absent, empty or someone else's — re-proved by
all six probes and the 40 assertions in the isolation suites, which check the
denials and not only the permissions.

## 59 foreign keys got the index they needed

A referential-integrity check runs *outside* RLS — it is about integrity, not
permission — so it can never be narrowed to one school. With no index leading on
the FK column it reads the whole child table.

| rows in the shared table | no leading index | with one |
|---|---|---|
| 360,000 | 4.96 ms | 0.17 ms |
| 3,600,000 | 106.64 ms | 1.08 ms |

Ten times the rows for twenty-one times the work. Removing one student fires
**fourteen** of these checks. The other side, measured on the same table:
~+4 µs per row inserted, +14% storage. 20 foreign keys are deliberately left
alone — configuration tables holding tens of rows per school — and that list is
now a named baseline in a guard rather than an accident.

`LibraryIssue.copyId` is the same shape that took the library service's own e2e
suite from 17 s to 823 s: its only index on the column is partial, and an RI
check has to see every row. That service wrote a guard so it could not come
back; this ports it to the product the library was a side project of.

## The gates that would have caught all of this never ran

`rls-coverage`, `tenant-isolation`, `route-coverage` and the authz suites all
live in `test:e2e`, and the `build` job has no database. They ran when somebody
remembered. `library-ci.yml` stands up a Postgres for exactly this reason; this
adds the school API's equivalent, and it is deliberately the whole suite rather
than a hand-picked subset.

It shows: `route-coverage` was **red** — 82 mounted routes were in neither authz
list (the whole Sports wing, session rollover, Celebrations, Records, the owner
lead desk), plus one entry naming a route that no longer exists. They go in the
weak list with the reason written down, so the debt is counted rather than
hidden: 233 of 528 routes are guarded and have no assertion saying who may call
them.

Two more things were in the way and are fixed: the suite read its JWT secrets,
SMTP host and S3 keys from the ambient shell (so it passed on one machine and
failed on the next, and could not run in CI at all), and two suites that need a
separately booted API failed 25 assertions instead of skipping — the exact noise
that trains people to ignore red.

## Also

`packages/library-db`'s `withOrg` spliced the org id into `SET LOCAL` instead of
binding it. The UUID check made it unexploitable, but `packages/db` has always
done both, and a regex alone is one careless refactor away from SQL injection
*at the tenancy boundary*.

`outbox-claim` was failing on `main` today in a full run and passing alone — its
copy of the drain's claim statement had no school predicate, so it counted rows
other suites left behind. Fixed in the copy only; the real drain stays
cross-tenant, because sweeping every school is its job.

## Verification

- Fresh database from all 95 migrations — applies clean, and the migration's own
  straggler check refuses to finish if any policy still casts a column.
- Deployed to staging first (#97) and verified live there: `isolation: enforced`,
  real tenant reads 148–320 ms, a token from one school 401s at another school's
  host and at an unknown host.
- Full e2e **951 passing, 0 failing** from a clean environment, locally and in CI.
- `pnpm preflight` green.
- 418 → 477 indexes. 127 policies through `app_current_tenant()`. 0 casting.

The migration and the deploy are independent here — no code references
`app_current_tenant()`, and old code works against the new policies — so either
order is safe. Production migration is still the manual `db-migrate` run.

author: phicks-debug
body:
## Summary

A turn with tool calls stored only its final step. The run persisted `response.messages`, which in AI SDK 7 is the last step alone, so tool calls and results never reached storage and the next turn had no memory of them. The dashboard hid it because its transcript comes from the live stream.

- Each step's new `responseMessages` are persisted in `prepareStep`, before steering is applied, and the rest in `onEnd`.
- Who gets the restored memory: on Anthropic, Google and every other provider, old tool calls are still pruned when history loads, exactly as before. The stored steps reach the model on OpenAI and Azure, on any agent with `session.pruning.enabled: false`, and they reach the compaction summary on every provider.
- On OpenAI and Azure, tool calls are no longer pruned while reasoning is kept. A pruned call would orphan its reasoning item.
- A tool call that history never answers (an approval the user walked away from, a step cut short) is dropped when history loads, together with that message's reasoning and item ids. Without this, OpenAI and Azure threw `AI_MissingToolResultsError` on every later turn until `/new`.
- Stored tool results drop inline bytes the way user messages already did, and one tool message shares a 768 KiB budget, so a screenshot or a huge MCP result can not pass Convex's 1 MiB row limit and end the run from inside `prepareStep`.
- The compaction limit measures the pruned context, the view the model gets. The summary still reads the full stored history, because the compaction prompt asks for tool outcomes and nothing reads those rows again afterwards.
- A step is written in one Convex mutation, `events: [{ cursor, event }]`, so a step boundary costs 4 round trips instead of 5 and a step is stored whole or not at all.

## Description

Stored conversations grow, and context is larger on OpenAI and Azure. A persist failure now fails the run instead of being swallowed. Older rows stay valid, so no reset.

Deploy order: Convex first, then core. Both `appendConversationEvent` mutations accept the new `events` array and the old single `cursor` + `event` args, because the core that is live while Convex rolls still sends the old shape and Convex rejects an unknown key outright. A new core against an old Convex would fail every conversation write. No schema change and no `_generated` diff.

Not covered: tool-call inputs are not capped, so a `write` call with a body over 1 MiB can still fail its row. On a pruning provider the compaction summary input can be larger than `maxContextLength`.

Docs: `apps/docs/docs/workspace/memory-and-session.md` and `apps/core/AGENTS.md` describe the tool-call rule for OpenAI and Azure.

## Verification

Focused: `tests/harness.test.ts`, `tests/context-management.test.ts`, `tests/message-metadata.test.ts` in `apps/core`, and `tests/runtimeIngress.test.ts` in `packages/convex`. One test runs the real `streamText` over two steps. The convex test goes through the convex-test harness, which enforces the arg validators.

`bun run --filter @broods/core check`, `bun run --filter @broods/convex check`, root `bun run lint` (exit 0), `bun run format:check`: all clean. Core suite `bun test --max-concurrency=1`: 1262 pass, 33 skip, 0 fail. Convex suite: 439 pass.

## Stack

Stack 18 of 26. Base: `fix/conversation-page-size`. Builds on #586. Merge in order; after a merge, retarget the next PR to `dev`.

The premise that these two compete for `main` turned out to be false. They collide on only four files, and none of them is app code — `app/index.html` and `app/voxelcraft/` never overlapped at all.

| File | Resolution |

The two newcomer guides already cross-referenced each other by branch name, so each keeps its full text at its own path with a status note explaining that its §1 branch layout is now history. author: davidtbilisi
body:
## Why

Tailwind v4 (`@tailwindcss/vite`) scans the whole repo for class names, and in dev a change to any scanned file makes Vite **reload every open page**. Saving a spec file while Playwright ran reloaded the app under the running tests and wiped the in-memory palace — the main cause of flaky runs while the UI specs were being repaired (#69).

## Change

One line in `src/index.css`:

```css
@source not "../tests";
```

## Evidence

A probe opens the app on a dev server, marks the page, touches a file, and checks whether the page survived:

| file saved | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `tests/ui/walk-mode.spec.ts` | page reloaded | **no reload** |
| `mcp-server/src/tools/routes.ts` | page reloaded | page reloaded (not excluded) |
| `src/app/navigationEvents.ts` (app code) | hot update | hot update |

Production build with and without the line: both CSS files (`index-*.css`, `vendor-tldraw-*.css`) are **byte-identical** — nothing under `tests/` is styled, so nothing that ships changes.

## Not changed

`mcp-server/` (and other folders the app doesn't style — `scripts/`, `docs/`, `src-tauri/`, …) are still scanned, so saving an MCP server file still reloads open pages. Excluding them works the same way if wanted.

Fixes #145

## What

Pin the native OpenAI Codex CLI in the shared agent image dependency closure — a pure two-file dep-pin diff:

- `agent-base/devbox.json`: add `"codex@latest"` (version-material line only).
- `agent-base/devbox.lock`: add the `codex@latest` entry.

The lock entry resolves through the directly reachable flake ref
`github:NixOS/nixpkgs/0a3468a402c449992505b6a9fc5b06580141b750#codex` (nixpkgs-unstable — already the lock's flake revision), committing the immutable 40-char revision plus the per-system store paths for all three Devbox systems (aarch64-darwin, aarch64-linux, x86_64-linux). No search-API dependency was used: the revision and the outPaths came from `nix eval github:NixOS/nixpkgs/<rev>#legacyPackages.<system>.codex.outPath`.

`codex` is the native OpenAI Codex CLI, not an unrelated same-name package: `meta.homepage = https://github.com/openai/codex`, `meta.mainProgram = codex`, `meta.description = "Lightweight coding agent that runs in your terminal"`.

## Acceptance (from the issue) and observed evidence

1. **Diff is only `agent-base/devbox.json` + `agent-base/devbox.lock`** — `git diff --stat`: `2 files changed, 40 insertions(+), 1 deletion(-)`.
2. **`devbox run -- codex --version` resolves the native executable from the committed lock** — run in `agent-base/`:

   $ devbox run -- codex --version
   codex-cli 0.154.0

   `devbox install` fetched exactly the committed x86_64-linux store path `/nix/store/w2k4sczcscass68x6j7z0qcgy0qdk1a0-codex-0.154.0`.
3. **Lock resolves an immutable Nixpkgs revision for all supported systems** — the entry carries the full revision `0a3468a402c449992505b6a9fc5b06580141b750` and store paths for aarch64-darwin / aarch64-linux / x86_64-linux; all three verified present on `cache.nixos.org` via `nix path-info --store https://cache.nixos.org`.

author: jerry73204
body:
Closes the last seven `gap` rows of the pubsub/service introspection area.
Both families were verdicted ADOPT / ADOPT-BOUNDED by the phase-417 pass; this
is the implementation, and all seven rows become `divergence` rather than
disappearing, because in each case a weakening remains and it is now WRITTEN
rather than discovered.

## Matched counts — 5 rows, all three languages

  * C `rcl_publisher_get_subscription_count(publisher, executor, out_count)`
    and `rcl_subscription_get_publisher_count(subscription, executor, out_count)`
  * C++ `Publisher<M>::get_subscription_count(Executor&, size_t*) const`
    and `Subscription<M>::get_publisher_count(Executor&, size_t*) const`
  * Rust `EmbeddedPublisher::get_subscription_count(&mut Executor)`
    and `Subscription::get_publisher_count(&mut Executor)`

Each forwards to the graph counter phase-381 W4 shipped, over the topic the
entity already remembers.

**TWO weakenings, both in the doc comment at every site.** THE QUESTION:
upstream counts the endpoints MATCHED to this entity — peers whose QoS is
compatible; we count every endpoint DISCOVERED on the topic, because that is
what the graph can answer and a backend with no QoS negotiation cannot tell the
two apart at all. Non-inverting in the SAFE direction: a topic nobody joined
still reads `0`, so "skip the work when nobody is listening" is answered
exactly, while an incompatible peer reads `1` where upstream reads `0` — you do
work nobody receives, never the reverse. THE RECEIVER: the executor is a
parameter, because we open one transport session per image and the Executor
owns it. Both are weakenings the compiler makes a porter notice, which is
RFC-0089's mechanical-edit test.

**And `Unsupported` is not `0`.** A backend that cannot read the graph returns
the error and does not write the out-parameter. Collapsing that into a count
would make a caller stop publishing on a backend that simply cannot tell.

## `*_info_by_topic` — 2 rows, the graph family's last forwarders

`NodeCtx::get_publishers_info_by_topic` / `get_subscriptions_info_by_topic`,
beside the ten forwarders the same phase landed. No behaviour: a one-line
delegation each. They stay `divergence` on SHAPE for the reason their ten
siblings in `graph.json` do — rclrs returns an owned `Vec<TopicEndpointInfo>`
and an owned container needs an allocator a 128 KiB target does not have, so we
stream through a visitor with every `&str` borrowed for the visit.

## Tests

`MockSession::with_graph` gained the endpoint-info slot, and it answers the two
sides DISTINGUISHABLY — different node name, different type, and the
`is_publisher` flag echoed — because ONE backend slot serves both entry points
and the only thing separating them is a `bool`. That is the defect a forwarder
of this shape has, and a fixture answering the same row either way cannot see
it.

- `the_matched_counts_reach_their_own_graph_counter` — the canned counts differ
  (3 vs 7), so a publisher wired to the publisher counter fails.
- `the_endpoint_info_forwarders_reach_their_own_side`.
- `a_backend_with_no_graph_does_not_report_a_count_of_zero` and
  `the_endpoint_info_forwarders_do_not_collapse_unsupported_into_empty` — the
  plain `MockSession` keeps the trait default, which is what XRCE reports.

Mutation-verified, each red on its own:
- `get_publishers_info_by_topic` forwarding to the subscription side
  (`left: "/endpoint/subscriber_node"`)
- `get_subscription_count` reaching `count_publishers` (`left: 3, right: 7`)

Compile probes extended rather than duplicated: the C++ pair joins
`entity_name_accessors.cpp` as method pointers (the weakening is in the
SIGNATURE, so the signature is what must not drift back) and the C pair joins
`graph_query_entry_points.c`, which exists because cbindgen once emitted no
declaration for four of five graph entry points while the Rust side stayed
green.

## Deliberate: the unsafe census grows by 2

`nros-c: unsafe extern 417 -> 419` — the two new C entry points, and nothing
else. Baseline re-written with `scripts/check-unsafe-census.py --write-baseline`
(issue 1221: the point is that a new unsafe site is a decision someone made).

## Ledger: 41 gap rows -> 34

All seven `gap` -> `divergence` (`adopt-bounded`). One new ours-only row,
`rust:Subscription::get_publisher_count`, filed `extension`: rclrs exposes no
publisher count on a subscription while rcl and rclcpp both do, which is the
same shape as `rust:Publisher::assert_liveliness`.

## Lane

Run in the `ros2` distrobox. `check::cli-fresh` ok, `check::fast` ok (339
gates), `check::build` 21 of 22 — the single red is `check-scaffold-builds`,
which is **issue 1448**, a pre-existing red on `main` reproduced identically on
two other branches and filed in the parent PR. The three steps that red
withdraws were run directly on this tree and are green: `just check api-parity`,
`just test-unit` and `just test-lane-contracts`. `scripts/api-parity.py --check`
and `--self-test` both pass.

Stacked on #1173 (`feat/444-name-accessors`): it adds the `topic_name()` these
counts read, and both touch `handles.rs`, `mock.rs` and `pubsub.json`. Retarget
to `main` once that merges.

author: dbeihl-utilicast
body:
## Intent

Fix the supervision watcher. It is degrading fleet supervision and has been all afternoon. Measured, not assumed: the liveness beacon can be one minute old, so supervision IS working at that moment. The fault is intermittent and has three shapes that may share a cause.

1. A false FAILED. The arm correctly evicted a watcher whose heartbeat was stale for 612 seconds, started a replacement, printed 'started pid=87926 (beacon fresh)', then declared 'FAILED - watcher cycle exited 1 without an actionable reason' and fired the full broken-supervision banner on a healthy system. A quiet cycle with nothing to report is being read as failure. The banner tells the reader not to arm manually and to investigate before ending. A false version of that trains the next agent to ignore a real one.

2. Repeated stale episodes. 'watcher still down, last beat 363s / 374s / 398s / 511s ago, grace 300s' many times in one day, each time recovering on its own. The beat is lapsing past its grace window regularly rather than once. Establish WHY: a slow cycle, a blocking read, a remote call that hangs, or the grace window being too tight for what a cycle now does. If it is real slowness rather than a bug, say so plainly and propose the honest fix, whether that is a wider grace window, a faster cycle, or a beat written independently of the cycle's work.

3. Two watcher processes existed simultaneously, seconds apart, from the eviction-and-restart path. Two watchers means duplicate wakes and duplicate supervision turns. Establish whether the eviction path can leave a duplicate, and make it leave exactly one.

No GitHub Actions workflow.

## What Changed
- Bound remote pending-reply observations to half the watcher freshness grace and refresh the liveness beacon after each completed observation.
- Require both stale beacon and lock claim before eviction, and preserve eviction handoff identity so quiet replaced watcher exits attach to a verified successor instead of reporting failure.
- Document the revised watcher continuity contract and add coverage for successor attachment, fresh replacement protection, and bounded remote observation.

## Risk Assessment

✅ Low: The fix is bounded to eviction handoff classification, stale-lock qualification, and remote-observation liveness, with concrete behavioral regression coverage for each changed race path.

## Testing

Ran the focused watcher-lock executable suite, which exercised real watcher and arm processes through stale-holder eviction, two-watcher races, quiet nonzero eviction handoff, fresh-replacement protection, and bounded remote-observation behavior; it completed successfully. Also launched the actual arm in an isolated local home and captured its fresh-beacon singleton startup. A real authorized remote endpoint was unavailable, so that transport-specific scenario remains untested live.

- Live validation: ⚠️ inconclusive - 4 of 5 scenarios driven live against the product

| Scenario | Result | Live | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| An operator arms supervision in an empty home and receives a started status only after the watcher owns the lock with a fresh beacon | ✅ pass | live | live-watcher-startup.log shows `watcher: started pid=2783457 (beacon fresh)`, matching lock PID, and beacon age 0 seconds. |
| Two concurrent stale-holder eviction attempts leave exactly one real watcher and the losing process reports the winner rather than a false failure | ✅ pass | live | `bash tests/fm-watcher-lock.test.sh`; artifact records `two real watchers racing to evict the same stale holder never produce a false FAILED escalation`. |
| When an evicted watcher resumes, handles TERM as a quiet rc=1 exit, and another arm establishes a fresh replacement, the original arm attaches instead of emitting a false FAILED banner | ✅ pass | live | `bash tests/fm-watcher-lock.test.sh`; artifact records `a non-actionable replaced cycle follows its healthy successor without a false FAILED banner`. |
| A fresh replacement cannot be evicted merely because it inherited its predecessor's old beacon timestamp | ✅ pass | live | `bash tests/fm-watcher-lock.test.sh`; artifact records `a fresh replacement cannot be evicted on the predecessor beacon's age`. |
| A remote pending-reply observation cannot allow its watcher beacon to age past the liveness grace | ⏸️ untested | no | No authorized remote secondmate endpoint or SSH credential is available in this environment. Provide an approved test remote host and credentials to drive `fm-on.sh ... observe` through the deployed t… |

author: kennethsinder
body: ## What changed Import resolution falls back to the importing file's own nearest project root when no acquired package snapshot contains that file. A path dependency is installed as a symlink to its own source tree, so a module reached through one canonicalizes outside the consumer's project root; every snapshot the caller acquired was filtered away and that module's own package imports resolved to nothing. The single-file resolver has always used the file's own root, so the two resolvers disagreed about one import, and the predicate census that refuses an unresolved import refused the whole consumer. ## Why Checking a consumer whose path dependency has its own dependency has refused since the census over imported evaluation sites landed (#8573). The census is not the defect; it is the first thing that asked whether a dependency's imports resolve, and the answer was already wrong. A git or registry dependency is copied inside the consumer's root and was never affected. ## The one risk The fallback runs only when every acquired snapshot has failed for the importing file, so a module that resolved before resolves the same way. A module no project provides still resolves to nothing; a control asserts that so the fallback cannot turn a missing module into a found one. A registry dependency at depth two is not measured, only the git and path shapes are. ## How the claim was verified Regression in the resolver's own test module: the outside-tree path dependency is the red-then-green case; an inside-tree path dependency and a copied dependency are positive controls; depth two through two symlinked hops resolves both hops; an import no project provides stays unresolved. With the fallback removed, the outside-tree case and both hops of the depth-two case fail while the copied, inside-tree and uninstalled-package controls stay green, so the fixture binds to this change rather than to something adjacent. A four-case probe against built binaries agrees with the unit cases. Closes #8573 --- Need help on this PR? Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need. Autofix is disabled.
